source.title: Compositionality and Ambiguity: Latent Co-occurrence and Interpretable Subspaces

record.tranche_reason: The study measures SAE-latent co-occurrence and how it changes with width, but does not test whether features in different-sized dictionaries correspond, split, partition the same inputs, or have nearby directions. Its discussion of splitting and absorption does not add results on those claims.
record.gate_note: The reported width-related co-occurrence and cluster-size results are recorded as related findings, not as tests of the claim versions: the study does not align features across SAE sizes or measure coarse-feature input coverage or direction. It also discusses possible composition and ambiguity, but those are not tests of feature splitting.
record.test_reason: The study measures how often SAE latents co-occur on the same token, and how co-occurrence clusters change with SAE width and L0, in GPT2-Small and Gemma-2-2b. It never matches latents across dictionary sizes, so it does not test whether coarse features split into finer ones, whether those cover the parent's inputs, or whether their directions lie close. Its mentions of splitting and absorption are speculation in the discussion. The Gemma number-word case is said to be 'may be related to feature absorption' but measures no parent/child firing failure. These are related findings, not tests of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Most latents are independent, but a minority co-occur in clusters mapping interpretable subspaces, through composition or ambiguity. Co-occurrence decreases as SAE width increases, and latents stay largely interpretable individually. The authors also argue some latents must be read as part of a cluster.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures Jaccard-normalized co-occurrence and cluster structure across SAE widths, with qualitative PCA case studies; it does not use cross-size feature matching or test feature-input partitioning and directional proximity.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported co-occurrence and cluster outcomes vary with SAE width; Gemma-2-2b cluster results are also discussed across different L0 settings.

fits_no_version.finding: In GPT2-Small (layer 8) and Gemma-2-2b (layer 12), per-token latent co-occurrence above chance decreases as SAE width grows. Co-occurrence cluster size and the fraction of latents in clusters also decrease, the latter then plateauing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider SAEs show less above-chance latent co-occurrence and fewer, smaller co-occurrence clusters.

fits_no_version.finding: In a 16k Gemma Scope SAE at layer 12, a similar 'of'-quantifier cluster appears at lower L0 (22 vs 80) and looks less compositional. Mean subgraph size also decreases with lower L0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lower-L0 SAEs show smaller co-occurrence clusters and less compositional encoding within them.

record.problems: The width-related findings are presented as aggregate trends without numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The cluster examples are selected through a non-exhaustive qualitative search. The study does not align latents across SAE sizes or test feature splitting directly.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for width-related co-occurrence or cluster trends were left out. Qualitative cluster examples and L0 comparisons were not included because they do not measure the cross-size feature-splitting behavior in the claim.

untested.parts: Whether coarse latents are replaced across widths by finer latents that cover their inputs and lie near their direction; no cross-size matching is done.
Splitting in larger models and open releases; the study uses open releases (the GPT2 feature-splitting set, Gemma Scope) but measures only co-occurrence.
Nested, geometrically close split families; the hierarchical fruit example is a hypothetical toy in future work.
Parent-latent firing failures and their dependence on size or sparsity; absorption is only suggested for the number-word cluster.
Decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, and novel latents appearing in larger SAEs.
Whether splitting is an objective artifact, and the effect of alternative objectives; the L1 local-code bias is argued, not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The study uses the Neuronpedia GPT2-Small 'feature splitting' SAE series, but only to measure co-occurrence across widths. The text's appeal to splitting and absorption is interpretive, not tested. The L0 comparisons are omitted from the rows, which the record declares, and they bear on no version. No numbers or uncertainty are reported for the width trends.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a coarse feature is replaced by finer features across SAE sizes, whether those features jointly cover its inputs, and whether their directions are nearby.
Whether the feature-splitting pattern holds at scale or across open SAE releases.
Whether split features form nested, geometrically close families that mirror a hierarchy of model concepts.
Whether parent latents fail to fire when child latents take over, and whether SAE size or sparsity changes that behavior.
Whether larger latents decompose into smaller-latent combinations and whether larger SAEs add novel latents.
Whether splitting is caused by the SAE objective, or whether alternative objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs change it.
